## Learning goals

1. Analyze a single categorical variable using the [binomial test]{.alert}, a type of null hypothesis significance test
2. Determine when to use a binomial test
3. Estimate uncertainty of a proportion

## Orange M&Ms

What is the probability of sampling 4 [orange]{.alert} M&Ms from a bag of 20 if $p = 0.2$ orange?

::: {.fragment}
Drawing a probability tree would be too hard.
:::

::: {.fragment}
"Fortunately" there's an equation!
:::

::: {.fragment}
$$\text{Pr}[X~\text{successes in}~n~\text{trials}] = {n \choose X} p^X (1 - p)^{(n - X)}$$
:::


## Binomial distribution {.top-align}

$$\text{Pr}[X~\text{successes in}~n~\text{trials}] = {n \choose X} p^X (1 - p)^{(n - X)}$$


- ${n \choose X}$: a count of the number of ways you could get $X$ successes in $n$ trials
- $p^X$: the probability of $X$ "successes" (multiplication rule)
- $(1-p)^{n-X}$: the probability of $n - X$ "failures" (multiplication rule)

## Binomial distribution

> The **binomial distribution** provides the probability distribution for the number of "successes" in a fixed number of independent trials, when the probability of success is the same in each trial.

Assumptions:

* the number of trials ($n$) is fixed
* separate trials are independent, and
* the probability of "success" ($p$) is the same in every trial

## Binomial distribution

$$\text{Pr}[X~\textit{successes}] = {n \choose X} p^X (1 - p)^{(n - X)}$$

- ${n \choose X}$: a count of the number of ways you could get $X$ successes in $n$ trials
- $p^X$: the probability of $X$ "successes" (multiplication rule)
- $(1-p)^{n-X}$: the probability of $n - X$ "failures" (multiplication rule)


## Summary

The [binomial distribution]{.alert} describes the probability of all possible outcomes from $n$ trials with probability of success $p$

Therefore, it is a [sampling distribution]{.alert} from a sample size of $n$ from a population where a proportion $p$ of the population is one discrete value (e.g. orange)

## M&Ms are fun and all...

But what are some biologically relevant examples?

::: {.incremental}
- Does a certain species prefer one habitat over another? [test statistic:]{.alert} number of occurrences in first habitat type versus the other
- Is a certain class of gene clustered on one chromosome? [test statistic:]{.alert} count of genes in the class on a specific chromosome versus all other chromosomes
- What is the dietary preference of some species? [test statistic:]{.alert} count of times the species ate one food type versus another
:::

## [Null Hypothesis Significance Testing]{.alert}

1. State $H_0$ and $H_\mathrm{A}$
2. Calculate the test statistic
3. Generate the null distribution
4. Calculate the $P$-value
5. Decide:
    - Reject $H_0$ if $P$-value $\le \alpha$
    - Fail to reject $H_0$ if $P$-value $> \alpha$

## $H_0$ and $H_A$ deal with [proportions]{.alert}

> A [proportion]{.alert} is the fraction of individuals having a particular attribute.

$$p = \frac{\text{Number of "successes"}}{\text{Number of trials}}$$

::: {.fragment}
**Example:** 21 out of 30 peʻelua pulelehua Kamehameha chose māmaki over *Urtica*, so the [estimated]{.alert} proportion is $\frac{21}{30}=0.7$
:::

::: {.fragment}
Note: The true proportion is a [population parameter]{.alert}, and we can [estimate]{.alert} it from data
:::

## Parameter and estimate

 Parameter | Estimate
:---------:|:--------:
 $p$       | $\hat{p}$

- $H_A$: The proportion of times peʻelua pulelehua Kamehameha choose māmaki versus *Urtica* will not be 0.5
:::

## Food preferences of the pulelehua Kamehameha caterpiller


- $H_0$: The true population proportion $p = 0.5$
- $H_A$: The true population proportion $p \ne 0.5$

::: {.fragment}
- [Test statistic]{.alert}: (# times chose māmaki) = 21 out of 30
:::

::: {.fragment}

::: {.pause-think}
What is the [null distribution]{.alert}?
:::

:::

::: {.fragment}
The null distribution is the [binomial distribution]{.alert} with $p = 0.5$
:::


## Food preferences of the pulelehua Kamehameha caterpiller

::: columns
::: {.column width="40%"}
$p = 0.5$

$n = 30$ trials


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](06-proportions-slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-11-1.png){fig-align='center' width=5in}
:::
:::


:::

::: {.column width="60%"}



::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# number of trials
n <- 30 

# number of times chose māmaki
x_success <- 21 

# null hypothesis proportion
p <- 0.5 

# P-value
upper <- pbinom(x_success - 1, size = n, prob = p,
                lower.tail = FALSE)

lower <- pbinom(n - x_success, size = n, prob = p,
                lower.tail = TRUE)

pval <- upper + lower

pval
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0.04277395
```


:::
:::


:::

:::

## Food preferences of the peʻelua pulelehua Kamehameha

- $H_0$: The true population proportion $p = 0.5$
- $H_A$: The true population proportion $p \ne 0.5$
- Test statistic: (# times chose māmaki) = 21 out of 30
- The null distribution is the [binomial distribution]{.alert} with $p = 0.5$

::: {.fragment}
- With $P$-value = 0.043 we **reject** the null at $\alpha = 0.05$ significance
:::


## Confidence Interval of a proportion

Remember, $\hat{p}$ (the proportion) is a sample estimate of the population parameter. Like any estimate we can calculate a confidence interval. But...

::: {.fragement}
The 2 SE rule does not work for 95% Confidence Intervals of the binomial distribution.
:::

## Confidence Interval of a proportion

The 2 SE rule does not work for 95% Confidence Intervals of the binomial distribution. So...

::: {.fragment}

We use R code instead


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
n <- 30
x_success <- 21

# P-value and 95% CI
binom.test(x_success, n)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

	Exact binomial test

data:  x_success and n
number of successes = 21, number of trials = 30, p-value = 0.04277
alternative hypothesis: true probability of success is not equal to 0.5
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.5060410 0.8526548
sample estimates:
probability of success 
                   0.7 
```


:::
:::
